Competition on Benchmarking Niching
Methods for Multimodal Optimization

Abstract
This report presents the experimental setup for the GECCO’2024 com-
petition on benchmarking niching methods on multimodal optimization.
1
1 Introduction
Multimodal optimization (MMO) aims to detect all high-quality solutions to
an optimization problem [1]. Without loss of generality, we frame this as a
minimization problem in this document, so as such this task includes identify-
ing all global minima (if there are more than one) and also high-quality local
minima. MMO methods are generally formed by augmenting a global search
method, commonly an evolutionary algorithm (EA) or swarm-based method,
with a diversity-enhancing technique [2]. These methods aim to detect a di-
verse set of high-quality solutions that can be helpful in the decision-making
process [3].
2 Test Problems
Although high-quality local minima, as long as they are diverse, can be desired
in many practical situations, this competition considers only problems with
multiple global minima in which an MMO method should ideally detect all
global minima with a predefined accuracy.
A set of 8 tunable composite functions are set out in this study. These
functions have been created by adapting and improving the procedure pro-
posed in [4], and the idea of grouping MMO challenges into global optimization
challenges and MMO-specific challenges [5, 6]. These composite functions were
intended to address some limitations of the widely adopted CEC’2013 test prob-
lems for MMO [7], including their limited scalability, low dimensionality, and
limited capability to differentiate MMO methods since many of these problems
are too easy for today’s competitive MMO methods.
Each of our eight composite functions is employed with two different settings
for its tunable parameters, resulting in 16 MMO problems that can be classified
into two groups:
 Group A: these MMO problems (PID = 1 , 2,..., 8) focus on evaluating
the capability of an MMO method in dealing with those challenges that
are peculiar to MMO, such as the presence of a higher number of global
minima with non-uniform distribution.
 Group B: these MMO problems (PID = 9 , 10,..., 16) focus on an MMO
method’s capability in dealing with both types of challenges, which in-
cludes challenges shared with global optimization (e.g., deceptive local
minima, ill-conditioning, and a weak global structure [8]) and MMO-
specific challenges.
Table 1 presents the specification of the test problems used in this compe-
tition. All of them should be treated as black-box problems for optimization
purposes. They are all deterministic; however, the procedure to create them
involves some randomness. To moderate the effect of this randomness, we cre-
ate and store different instances of each MMO benchmark problem, denoted

3 Simulation Settings
The participating methods should report their results on
 16 test problems ( PID = 1, 2,...,..., 16), as presented in Table 1,
 4 different problem dimensionalities: D = 2, 5, 10, 20,
 15 problem instances per PID and D (PIN = 1, 2,..., 15), and
 one run for each PID, each PIN, and each D.
The total number of optimization runs would be 16 × 15 = 960. For all
problems:
 Evaluation budget is⌊50, 000D⌋
 The search space is [−5, 5]D
Using a single CPU core, the time required for all solution evaluations is
about 16 hours. A typical MMO solver should take about 30-40 hours to com-
plete all simulations using one core.
3
4 Performance Metric
A score is calculated for the performance of each participating method on each
problem. This score is the average of two indicators. The first one is the
well-known peak ratio (PR), which is defined as the fraction of global minima
that have been detected given the target accuracy in the objective space ( ϵf =
f(x)−f ∗). The second indicator is the F1 score:
F1 = 2× Precision× Recall
Precision + Recall (1)
In the context of MMO, recall is the fraction of global minima from the existing
global minima that have been detected by the algorithm. It is mathematically
equal to PR. Precision is the ratio of the detected global minima to the number
of solutions reported/provided by the algorithm [3]. The F− 1 score is cal-
culated over the final reported/provided solutions by an algorithm, therefore,
it is identical to the static F1 score used in CEC’2013 competition on niching
methods for MMO [7].
Five values forϵf are considered: ϵf = 10−1, 10−2, 10−3, 10−4, 10−5. PR and
static F1 are calculated for each problem with respect to each value of ϵf. The
overall score of a method is the average of all these 2× 5× 960 = 9600 numbers.
5 Parameter Setting for the Participating Meth-
ods
Each MMO method has some control parameters that should be set. In this
competition, ad-hoc parameter tuning is not allowed; however, the following
features of the problems are assumed to be known a priori, and thus, they can
be used for parameter setting:
 Problem dimensionality D
 Search space bounds
 The evaluation budget
 Desired tolerance for approximation of the global minimum ϵtight
f = 10−5,
ϵloose
f = 10−1
Other information such as the global minimum value, the number of existing
global minima (NGM), PID, PIN, and random seed number may NOT be used
for parameter tuning. This information may NOT be used by the algorithm
for optimization either. The participant should explicitly state what informa-
tion has been used for parameter setting. They are also encouraged (but not
required) to elaborate on how such information was used for parameter setting.
They should also report the total time that all 960 simulations take in their
report.
4
The participants should avoid tuning the random seed number and use a
reasonable predefined set of seed numbers, e.g., 1 , 2,..., 15 for 15 PINs of each
PID and each D.
6 Result Files
For each PID, each PIN, and each D, one CSV file should be provided. The
name of the file should be pid** pin** dim**.csv. For example, for PID=5,
PIN=4, and D = 20, the name of the file should be pid05 pin04 dim20.csv.
These files should be submitted in a zipped folder.
Data in each file should be the reported solutions by the MMO method,
i.e., those solutions deemed by the MMO method to be distinct global minima,
where each row represents a solution. For the ith row, the firstD columns store
the decision parameters of the ith reported solution. Column D + 1 stores the
solution fitness calculated by the method. Columns D + 2 and D + 3 show the
evaluation and the time (in milliseconds) at which the solution has been found,
respectively. Columns D + 2 and D + 3 are optional. Notably, only solutions
(columns 1, 2,...,D ) are used for the calculation of the performance indicator,
so the participants should make sure that solutions are reported with sufficient
precision.
7 Using the Code
The code of the composite functions is written in a way that it can easily be
integrated with an MMO method. The following explains the usage of the code:
 Step 1: The following line creates the problem object and sets the values
for all tunable parameters of the benchmark problem based on the problem
ID (PID), problem instance number (PIN), and problem dimensionality
(D):
problem=ProblemMM(PID, PIN, D)
 Step 2: The following command creates and stores all data related to the
problem.
problem.form()
 Step 3: The following command evaluates a solution
problem.eval(x) calculates the fitness of the solution x
The object problem has some useful attributes, such as:
 problem.countEval, which returns the number of solution evaluations
so far.
 problem.maxEval returns the evaluation budget
 problem.globMinX (only for post-processing of the results) returns the
global minima.
